paras: The bombing of William Austin's home was a dynamite attack in mid-June 1919 on the Lake Shore Drive residence of William Austin, a Chicago man who owned South Side property occupied by Black tenants. Black papers tied the explosion, which damaged the house, to an anonymous warning that Austin get rid of his "Colored" tenants.

By June the Chicago Defender counted repeated bombings of South Side homes, including the house at 4807 Grand boulevard occupied by Mrs. Harrison's family. Austin, a former president of the Hamilton Club, said he owned that house. He told the Defender that on a Sunday an unidentified person had told him "to get rid of the Colored people occupying my property."

According to the Defender, on a Monday night bombers placed a dynamite time explosive under Austin's basement at 103 Bellevue avenue, doing "much damage." A Chicago dispatch in the Omaha Monitor placed the bomb near the "Gold Coast" residence of "William D. Austin, broker," breaking windows for blocks but doing "minor damages to property."

Austin vowed to spare neither time nor expense until the bombers "and the higher-ups behind them" were brought to justice. Alderman Louis B. Anderson said he was working with the police and named the "Kenwood Improvement Association," formed for "keeping undesirable people out of the community," as a suspect. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

The bombing appeared in two Chicago Defender items on June 21 and in the Omaha Monitor on June 26 under "BOMB THROWERS AT WORK AGAIN." The Defender's longer piece praised Austin's belief in "fair play, common sense and justice" and called the bombers "anarchist performers." Its shorter item was cooler, saying Austin "styled himself" the owner and faulting property owners eager to sell "at fabulous sums" for aiding "a social disorder."

The reports differ on the night (Monday or Tuesday), the address (103 Bellevue avenue or 108 Bellevue place), Austin's middle initial and occupation, and the extent of damage. The shorter Defender item also doubted Austin's claim to own 4807 Grand boulevard rather than its occupant, Mrs. Richard B. Harrison.

reader.title: Bombing of William Austin's home
bases: A bomb was exploded under or near Austin's home after he was warned to remove Black tenants from his South Side property (A4, A5, A6).

The Chicago Defender (A4, A5) and a separately worded Chicago dispatch in the Omaha Monitor (A6) agree that Austin's Lake Shore Drive / Gold Coast home was bombed after a warning about his Black tenants, though they differ on day, address and damage.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender main account
accounts.gist: Bombers put dynamite in a time explosive under the basement of Austin's home at 103 Bellevue avenue on Monday night, doing much damage; Austin vowed to hunt the bombers and those behind them.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender short item
accounts.gist: The explosion came Tuesday night at 108 Bellevue place as an attempt to intimidate Attorney William B. Austin, who said an unknown caller had told him on a Sunday to get rid of his Colored tenants; the writer doubted Austin owned the house.

accounts.label: Chicago dispatch (Omaha Monitor)
accounts.gist: A bomb exploded near the Gold Coast residence of William D. Austin, broker, breaking windows for blocks with minor damage, believed to follow a telephone warning to get rid of his Negro tenants.

framing.detail: The Defender's page-20 piece praised Austin as a believer in 'fair play, common sense and justice', called the bombers 'anarchist performers' and quoted Bancroft calling bomb throwing 'wholly un-American'.
The Defender's page-16 item said Austin 'styled himself' the owner and blamed property owners selling 'at fabulous sums' for aiding 'a social disorder'.
The Omaha Monitor ran a brief dispatch under 'BOMB THROWERS AT WORK AGAIN', linking the bomb to repeated explosions in South Side buildings occupied by Negroes.

conflicts.note: A5 also says Austin was interviewed Tuesday, which fits a Monday bombing better; both are in the same Defender issue.
